summary: Teach a/b as a COUNT of unit fractions 1/b: 3/5 is 'three one-fifths', 7/4 is 'seven one-quarters'. The pivotal move is letting the count pass the whole — iterating 1/4 past 4/4 = 1 to 5/4, 6/4, 7/4, landing exactly on 1 3/4 — so improper fractions appear as the ordinary continuation of counting equal units on the number line, not a strange new object. This unit-as-building-block view seeds like-denominator addition (join the counts), multiplication (a/b = a × 1/b), and mixed numbers.
misconceptions: Believing a fraction must be less than 1, so an improper fraction like 7/4 'isn't a real/proper number' or must be an error.
Adding denominators when joining unit fractions: 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 rather than 2/4.
Whole-number bias in placing improper fractions: reading 7/4 as near 7 (or treating the 7 as the dominant number) rather than as seven quarters just past 1 3/4.
Losing the unit: writing 3/5 = 1/5 + 1/5 + 1/5 but unable to say the denominator stays 5 because each part is the same size 1/5.
Thinking the number line 'stops' at 1 for fractions, so not continuing the jumps past the whole.

activities.title: Stamp the unit-fraction jumps and cross the whole
steps: Work on a number line marked 0 to 2 with whole-number anchors at 1 and 2.
Add one 1/4 jump at a time starting from 0, saying each landing aloud: 'one quarter, two quarters, three quarters'.
Keep a running record that shows BOTH the count (number of copies) and the value n/4, alongside a growing equation 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 ...
On the fourth jump, notice the marker lands exactly on 1 and the tally reads 4/4; then deliberately keep going — tap again to step to 5/4, past the whole, still a definite point on the line.
Continue to the seventh jump, landing exactly on 1 3/4, with the equation showing seven 1/4's and the side note 7/4 = 1/4 × 7.

Switch the unit to 1/3 and repeat while keeping the whole-number anchors 1 and 2 fixed, counting up to six jumps (6/3 = 2) on this 0–2 line. To continue to seven jumps (7/3 = 2 1/3), extend the line past 2 first. Each jump is now larger: three third-jumps reach the same point 1 that four quarter-jumps reached.
activities.insight: A fraction a/b is just a count of equal units 1/b; nothing forces the count to stop at the whole, so improper fractions like 7/4 are ordinary points on the line. The denominator names the size of the unit you are counting.

activities.title: Walk through a pre-built iteration and read the decomposition
steps: Study a 0–2 number line showing seven quarter-jumps, revealing the running total jump by jump (1/4, 2/4, ... 7/4).
At the 4/4 mark, read the flap '= 1 whole, keep going' and continue tracing to 7/4.
Read the side card showing 7/4 = 1/4 × 7 and 7/4 = 1 3/4.
Lay out seven identical quarter-tiles end to end and match them to the seven jumps, then state in words that each part is the same size 1/4.
activities.insight: Seven copies of 1/4 decompose 7/4, the count continues naturally past 1, and 7/4 equals exactly 1 3/4 — the same unit-count read from a worked layout.

activities.title: Predict-then-check: where do seven quarter-jumps land?
steps: Before making any jumps, PREDICT where seven jumps of 1/4 from 0 will land — before 1, exactly on 1, or past 1 — and state WHY.
Iterate the seven quarter-jumps, crossing 4/4 = 1 and landing exactly on 1 3/4.
Explain any mismatch between the prediction and the result.

Answer probing questions: Why doesn't 7/4 land near 7 when there's a 7 in it? If it were 7/3 instead of 7/4, would the jumps be bigger or smaller, and would you land further from or closer to 0, and why? When you write 7/4 as seven 1/4's, why does the bottom number stay 4 and not grow? At the fourth jump you reached exactly 1 — what is that point as a fraction, and why doesn't counting have to stop there?
Write 7/4 as a sum of unit fractions and answer: is 7/4 a real number, and how do you know?
activities.insight: Stating a reason, not just a landing spot, reveals whether the learner holds the fraction-must-be-less-than-1 belief or the add-denominators error, and distinguishes a lucky correct placement from genuine understanding that 7/4 is a count of seven units.

activities.title: Spot and refute the add-denominators move
steps: Consider the claim 1/4 + 1/4 = 2/8 and test it on the number line by making two equal quarter-jumps from 0.
Mark where the two jumps actually land and compare it with where 2/8 would sit.
State in your own words why joining two copies of the same unit gives 2/4, not 2/8.

Answer a quick check: 5/8 = 1/8 + 1/8 + __ (fill the remaining 1/8 terms to make five eighths — three more are needed); then order 3/4, 5/4, 7/4, 9/4 on a line long enough to reach 9/4 (use a 0–3 line, since 9/4 = 2 1/4 lies past 2).
activities.insight: Joining unit fractions keeps the unit (denominator) fixed and adds the counts (numerators); the jumps stay the same size.

checkQuestion: Show 7/4 on a number line from 0 to 2 by making equal jumps, and write 7/4 as a sum of unit fractions. Then tell me: is 7/4 a real number, and how do you know?
checkAnswer: Seven equal jumps of 1/4 from 0, landing at 1 3/4; 7/4 = 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4 + 1/4. Yes, 7/4 is a real number — it is seven quarters, a definite point just past 1 3/4 on the line.
